newsitem.title: USA: No crisis for Mexican peso, but volatility remains.
newsitem.headline: No crisis for Mexican peso, but volatility remains.

text.p: The currency crisis that wreaked havoc on the Mexican economy two years ago may have receded in memory, but investors are not letting down their guard.

Emerging market debt experts here agree that the free-floating peso is unlikely to run into a colossal devaluation, but periodic adjustments to inflation and interest rates as well as sensitivity to political changes could bring choppiness.
"We are going to see a more stable peso in 1997 as inflation continues to go down," said Jaime Valdivia, vice president of emerging market research at Morgan Stanley.
The Mexican government has projected an inflation target of 15 percent for 1997, which Valdivia thinks is reachable,
"The peso is going to be in line with the inflation differential," he said, noting that in nominal terms, the peso would slide, but in real term it should remain constant for 1997.

As implied in the peso's forward rates, the market currently expects the currency to end 1997 at 9 to 10 per dollar, assuming the interest rate at 17-1/2 percent, Valdivia said. The peso was quoted 7.862/872 at 1330 EST.

Thanks to the restrictive monetary and fiscal policy adopted by the Mexican government, the peso withstood a brief turbulence in October and held well in the fourth quarter when the currency usually comes under some pressure, said Arturo Porzecanski, chief economist of fixed income research as ING Barings.
The trend bodes well for 1997, he said, forecasting the peso rate to average 8.7 to the dollar for the year, and 9.3 at the end of the year.
Despite general calmness, the peso tends to move in "step-like" fashion, stable for weeks or even months, then hops and skids lower,
Porzecanski predicted a few bumps in the second quarter ahead of the Congressional election in July as foreign investors might choose to stay on the sidelines.
In addition, with the recovery of the Mexican economy, consumer demand for import goods could push up the dollar and weaken the peso, he said.

Some of the peso's volatility stems from the way the Mexican central bank uses monetary base as its instrument of monetary management, which leads to volatility in interest rates and capital inflow and in turn affects the exchange rate, said Valdivia.

But such adjustments should not affect the fundamental imrprovements in Mexico's credit, he said, adding that he expected an upgrade of the sovereign credit from its current Ba2 by Moodys Investors Service and BB by Standard and Poor's by the end of 1997.
The peso's strength cannot be considered in isolation in the increasingly integrated global capital markets, said Gary Evans, emerging market debt strategist at Lehman Brothers.
Lest one forget, he said, the current liqudity boom traces back to the Mexican rescue package as well as to the large interest rate cuts in Japan and Germany.
As the liqudity remains ample going into 1997, the Mexican peso looks solid, although a strong currency may not be all that good for Mexico's export performance, Evans said.
Currency traders said investors with large peso exposures have not relaxed with this upbeat outlook and the hedging remains expensive.
"People don't wake up one day and find the peso like the Canadian dollar," said a trader with a money center bank.
Even in a relatively smooth year in 1996, the historical volatility for the peso averaged 11.45 percent, compared to 4.35 percent for the Canadian dollar, he said.
